title: Cornrows vs Box Braids for Men
hero_alt: Man holding a bundle of long box braids over one shoulder
card_text: Cornrows lie flat in rows. Box braids hang free from square parts. Length, chair time and the look, side by side.
lede: Cornrows are braided flat against the scalp in rows, so the braid and the part lines run together across the head. Box braids are separate braids, each starting from its own square section of scalp and hanging free. Cornrows work on shorter hair and keep a tight, close shape; box braids need more length and move like loose hair.
The photo above is a cornrow set from my chair. Here's how the two styles compare, and how to ask about either one before you book.

blocks.heading: Flat rows or free braids.
blocks.lead: It starts with how the hair is parted.

subsections.heading: Cornrows
paragraphs: Each cornrow picks up hair as it travels along a part, so the braid stays attached to the scalp from start to finish. The parts are long lines, straight back, curved, or angled toward the crown. The finished shape sits close to the head, almost like a pattern drawn on it.

subsections.heading: Box braids
paragraphs: Box braids start by dividing the scalp into a grid of small squares. Each square becomes one braid that leaves the scalp and hangs down on its own. The parts show as a checkerboard, and the braids can be worn down, pulled back or tied up.

blocks.heading: How they compare.
rows: More, braids need room to hang
Depends on how long the braids hang

blocks.heading: How much hair you need.
paragraphs: Because a cornrow travels along the scalp and gathers hair as it goes, it can work with less length than a braid that has to hang on its own. That's a big reason cornrows are common on men who keep their sides short.

Box braids look their part when they have some length to fall. On short hair they can end up stubby and stick out instead of lying down. Extension hair is often added to box braids for that reason, which is a different kind of appointment.
If you're growing your hair out for braids, tell me where you're at. A photo of your hair right now, from the top and the back, makes that conversation easy.

blocks.heading: The sets in my photos.
blocks.lead: Rows, a fade and a little gold.
paragraphs: The braids on my site are cornrow sets: rows running straight back, pairs that meet at the crown, and some finished with gold cuffs on the ends, like the one at the top of this post. Most sit over a faded or tapered side, so the rows stand out against clean skin.

Booksy lists Braids as personalized braiding styles, with the price shown as varies and {{minutes:braids}} set aside. If box braids are what you have in mind, text me a photo of the style before you book and ask. That way we both know what the appointment is before you clear the time for it.

blocks.heading: Plan for the time.
paragraphs: Either style is slow, careful work. Every part has to be clean and every braid even, and that doesn't happen in a quick visit. On Booksy, braids hold {{minutes:braids}}, so pick a morning or an afternoon when you aren't watching the clock.

Bring the photo you texted me, so we can look at it together before the first part goes in. If the style uses a fade underneath, say so when you book, so the sides and the rows are planned as one look.
Payment comes after the braids are done. Long bookings are hard to refill at short notice, so move or cancel on Booksy as soon as your plans change.

items.q: What's the main difference between cornrows and box braids?
items.a: Cornrows are braided flat to the scalp along long parts. Box braids are individual braids from square parts that hang loose.

items.q: Which works better on short hair?
items.a: Cornrows, usually, because they don't need length to hang. Box braids need more hair to lie down well.

items.q: Can I get braids with a fade?
items.a: Yes. Most of the sets in my photos pair braided rows with a faded or tapered side.
Booksy shows braids as varies, because the price changes with the style. Text me a photo and ask before you book.
